title: Maps, sets and two-pointer scans

objectives.text: Maintain a prefix frequency invariant and produce a deterministic count/tie-ordered report.
Prove pointer movement under a sorted or nonnegative input precondition instead of applying a pattern blindly.
Count occurrences passing through prefix nodes, including repeated whole words.
Use first-child/next-sibling arrays with bounded alphabet lookup and explicit memory cost.
Group anagram occurrences by a canonical key and prove deterministic member and group ordering, preserving repetitions.
Count unordered index pairs by querying complementary prefix multiplicities before inserting the current value.
Maintain key values and least-to-most-recent order through hits, misses, new writes and existing-key updates.

blocks.markdown: A map can accumulate multiplicities instead of overwriting records. Start counts empty. After each processed prefix, counts[s] equals the number of occurrences of symbol s in that prefix. For a new symbol, get(s,0) supplies zero before adding one. This does not silently replace missing financial data with zero: here zero is the explicitly defined count of occurrences before any have been seen. Symbols remain case-sensitive.

blocks.caption: Expected output: [('A', 2), ('B', 2), ('a', 1)], then []. The compound key (-count,symbol) orders count descending and ties by ASCII symbol ascending in this validated ASCII domain. Taking [:k] returns at most k distinct entries, not the first k input messages. A capital A and lowercase a are distinct keys.

Python Counter can count hashable objects too, but Counter.most_common tie order follows first encounter for equal counts, not automatically the lexicographic rule above. Choose and encode the required tie contract. Under ordinary expected hash-lookup assumptions, counting n messages takes expected O(n) map operations; sorting u distinct keys adds O(u log u) comparison work in the comparison model. Expensive/long keys and adversarial cases require more careful cost analysis. Expected hashing cost is not a worst-case constant-time guarantee.

For a sorted ascending integer sequence, look for two DISTINCT positions whose values sum to target. Keep left<right. If a[left]+a[right]<target, then a[left]+a[j] is too small for every j<=right, so left cannot participate in a remaining solution; increment left. If the sum is too large, a[i]+a[right] is too large for every i>=left; decrement right. If equal, a pair is found. Each move eliminates only positions proved impossible, and at most n positions move past a boundary.

blocks.caption: Expected output: True, then True, then False, then True. A single 4 cannot pair with itself; two 4 values at distinct positions can. This algorithm relies on sorted order but permits negative integers. Sorting an unsorted input first is additional work and may change caller order or index identity.

blocks.markdown: A window scan is a different pointer invariant. For nonnegative integers and a positive threshold, maintain total=sum(values[left:right+1]). Advance right to add an item. While the sum reaches the threshold, record the length and shrink from left to seek a shorter qualifying window. Removing a nonnegative item cannot increase the sum; adding one cannot decrease it. Both pointers only advance, giving linear total pointer movements. Report None when there is no qualifying nonempty window.

blocks.source:
def smallest_window_at_least(values, threshold):
    # Precondition: nonnegative integer values; strictly positive threshold.
    if type(threshold) is not int or threshold <= 0:
        raise ValueError("expected positive integer threshold")
    if any(type(value) is not int or value < 0 for value in values):
        raise ValueError("expected nonnegative integer values")
    left, total, best = 0, 0, None
    for right, value in enumerate(values):
        total += value
        while total >= threshold:
            length = right - left + 1
            best = length if best is None else min(best, length)
            total -= values[left]
            left += 1
    return best

print(smallest_window_at_least([2, 1, 3, 2], 5))
print(smallest_window_at_least([0, 0], 1))
blocks.caption: Expected output: 2, then None. Windows [3,2] and [2,1,3] qualify for threshold 5; the shortest qualifying length is 2. The code checks the nonnegative domain before running the pointer logic.

blocks.markdown: The nonnegative precondition is load-bearing. For values [1,-1,5] and threshold 5, blindly running this same shrink-only-when-qualified algorithm can record length 3 and then stop after removing 1 drops the sum to 4. It misses the valid length 1 window [5], because removing -1 would raise the sum again. Reject such input under this interface or choose a different algorithm. Two pointers are a proof obligation, not a magic speed template.

Prefix count invariant

There are 1 to 100000 words and queries; each word or prefix has 1 to 20 lowercase ASCII letters. Each distinct nonempty prefix is a trie node; the root represents the empty prefix internally. Insert every occurrence, not only distinct words. passed[node] counts occurrences beginning with that node's prefix. Increment after each character, including the terminal node. A word is its own prefix. No terminal marker is needed because this task does not ask exact-word membership, deletion or listing.

Sparse layout and transitions

Up to 2000001 nodes makes 26 Python references per node expensive. Four typed arrays store head (first child), sibling (next child of the same parent), passed (count), and label (incoming letter 0..25). -1 means missing. To follow a letter, scan the parent's child chain. Child labels are unique, so there are at most 26 checks. A missing insert creates one node and prepends it to head; a missing query returns 0. This is a sparse trie, not a sorted-word shortcut.

Proof and trace

One insertion increments precisely all prefixes of that occurrence, so induction preserves passed counts. A query walks its characters: a missing transition means no such stored prefix; otherwise read the final passed count. For [spy,spyder,spy,aapl,amzn], both sp and spy have count 3, a has count 2, and z has count 0. Prefix nodes need not be whole words. Deduplicating spy would wrongly reduce 3 to 2. For [a,ab,a], the counts are a: 3, ab: 1, abc: 0.

Bounds and typed-array semantics

Let S be inserted characters, Q query characters, and U distinct nodes including the root. Work is O(26*(S+Q)), linear for the fixed 26-letter alphabet. Space is O(U+n+q), including the supplied strings and output under the fixed length bound. S,Q<=2000000 and U<=2000001.

Array type i is guaranteed only a 2-byte minimum: use i when itemsize>=4, otherwise l (minimum 4 bytes). Node IDs<=2000000 and counts<=100000 fit signed 32-bit integers; labels use B. Array element payload is U*(3*integer_itemsize+label_itemsize), plus allocated capacity, objects, input and output. That is not exact process RAM. Array growth is amortized, not hard real time. Public prefixes are nonempty, so the root count need not be maintained.

Independent transfer

Compare with sum(word.startswith(prefix) for word in words), including repeats, whole words, missing deep branches and extensions beyond a word. Exercise 100000 twenty-letter words with many distinct prefixes and all-identical words, plus 100000 queries. Explain sibling-label lookup separately from node indexes. This does not claim Unicode, empty-prefix, erase, autocomplete or remote judge memory acceptance.

blocks.source:
MOD = 1000000007

def prefix_counts(words, prefixes):
    from array import array
    code = 'i' if array('i').itemsize >= 4 else 'l'
    (head, sibling, passed) = (array(code, [-1]), array(code, [-1]), array(code, [0]))
    label = array('B', [0])
    for word in words:
        node = 0
        for char in word:
            key = ord(char) - ord('a')
            child = head[node]
            while child != -1 and label[child] != key:
                child = sibling[child]
            if child == -1:
                child = len(head)
                head.append(-1)
                sibling.append(head[node])
                passed.append(0)
                label.append(key)
                head[node] = child
            node = child
            passed[node] += 1
    out = []
    for prefix in prefixes:
        node = 0
        for char in prefix:
            key = ord(char) - ord('a')
            child = head[node]
            while child != -1 and label[child] != key:
                child = sibling[child]
            node = child
            if node == -1:
                break
        out.append(str(passed[node] if node != -1 else 0))
    return out

print(prefix_counts(['spy', 'spyder', 'spy', 'aapl', 'amzn'], ['sp', 'spy', 'a', 'z']))
print(prefix_counts(['a', 'ab', 'a'], ['a', 'ab', 'abc']))
blocks.caption: Expected ['3', '3', '2', '0'], then ['3', '1', '0']. The compact sparse trie preserves multiplicity.

Equivalence needs a canonical key

Two lowercase tickers belong to the same family exactly when their sorted character strings match. Sorting forgets order but preserves each letter multiplicity, so equal keys are necessary and sufficient for anagrams. A set of letters would be wrong: ab and aab have the same set but different counts. The map value must be a list of occurrences, not a set, because duplicate tickers are retained.

Two different sorts define the output

First sort members of every family alphabetically. Then sort the families by decreasing occurrence count and, on a tie, by their first member. Distinct families cannot have the same first ticker, since that ticker determines its canonical family. For [ab,ba,aab,ab,b], family [ab,ab,ba] comes first, followed by [aab] then [b]. The count includes repeated ab.

Empty case, proof and cost

n=0 emits one line 0 with no group lines. Otherwise every occurrence is appended exactly once under its unique key and emitted exactly once. For n<=100000 and ticker length L<=20, key construction costs O(n L log L), with additional comparison sorting of members/groups. Character comparison itself can cost O(L), not an abstract zero-cost key. The function sorts new lists and does not mutate the supplied tickers. Test duplicates, singleton groups, tie order and same-letter-set/different-count counterexamples.

blocks.source:
from collections import OrderedDict, deque
from bisect import bisect_left
import heapq

def group_tickers(tickers):
    families = {}
    for ticker in tickers:
        key = ''.join(sorted(ticker))
        families.setdefault(key, []).append(ticker)
    groups = [sorted(group) for group in families.values()]
    groups.sort(key=lambda group: (-len(group), group[0]))
    return [str(len(groups))] + [' '.join(group) for group in groups]

print(*group_tickers(['ab', 'ba', 'aab', 'ab', 'b']), sep='\n')
print(*group_tickers([]))

State is a prefix multiset

Before processing position j, seen[x] counts exactly the earlier positions i<j with value x. Every earlier complement T-a[j] forms a unique valid pair ending at j. Add that count to pairs, then insert a[j]. This order enforces distinct indexes without special cases. Each pair has exactly one later endpoint, so no pair is lost or counted twice.

Duplicates are the point, not an exception

For T=4 and [2,2,2], contributions are 0,1,2 and the answer is 3. Inserting first would count each current 2 paired with itself. A boolean seen set would miss multiplicities. Negative values and negative targets are allowed; no monotone-window or positive-only assumption is available. This counts pairs of positions, not distinct value combinations.

Bounds, output and transfer

n<=100000. All equal values with target twice that value give n*(n-1)/2, up to 4999950000, exceeding signed32-bit range. Python integers retain it exactly. Expected hash work is O(n), O(u) state for u distinct values, and one returned decimal output line. This is expected hashing cost, not guaranteed constant time against arbitrary adversarial keys. Compare with the independent i<j double loop on small signed fixtures.

from collections import OrderedDict, deque
from bisect import bisect_left
import heapq

def count_pairs(T, a):
    seen = {}
    pairs = 0
    for value in a:
        pairs += seen.get(T - value, 0)
        seen[value] = seen.get(value, 0) + 1
    return [str(pairs)]

print(*count_pairs(4, [2, 2, 2]))
print(*count_pairs(0, [-1, 1, -1, 1]))

A lookup map alone does not encode recency

The cache has a value per key and an order from least recently used to most recently used. GET hit returns the value and moves that key to the MRU end. GET miss returns MISS and leaves all state unchanged. PUT writes/updates the value and makes that key MRU. A plain insertion-ordered dict does not automatically move an existing key when its value is reassigned.

OrderedDict implements the needed transitions

Use OrderedDict with LRU at the left and MRU at the right. On a GET hit, read before move_to_end(key). On PUT, assign then move_to_end(key), and if len(cache)>capacity remove popitem(last=False). An existing-key update never grows the key count, so cannot cause an eviction by itself. The parser supplies PUT values as strings; int(operation[2]) is the explicit declared integer parse before storing.

Trace, invariant and cost

With capacity 2: PUT A 1, PUT B 2, GET A makes order B,A; PUT C 3 evicts B; GET B is MISS; PUT A 4 changes A and makes it MRU; GET A prints 4. After every operation, key count<=capacity and recency order contains each live key exactly once. Expected hash/endpoint work is O(1) per operation under normal key assumptions, O(capacity) state and O(number of GETs) output for up to 100000 operations. A vector search/shift would be linear. This is a single-threaded simulation, not a concurrent or distributed cache.
